title: Conformal Prediction Covers on Average. That Is Rarely What You Wanted.
summary: A split conformal interval at level alpha = 0.1 will contain the truth 90% of the time. The statement is exactly true, finite-sample, and requires almost nothing of your model. It is also doing far less work than most people deploying...
body:
A split conformal interval at level $\alpha = 0.1$ will contain the truth 90% of the time. The statement is exactly true, finite-sample, and requires almost nothing of your model. It is also doing far less work than most people deploying conformal prediction believe, because the averaging in "90% of the time" runs over the test covariate $X_{n+1}$ along with everything else. A procedure that covers every easy case and fails on every hard one satisfies the guarantee precisely.

That gap between marginal and conditional coverage is not a footnote. It is the organizing constraint of the entire field, it is provably not fixable in the distribution-free setting, and nearly everything interesting in conformal prediction over the last seven years — quantile-based scores, Mondrian calibration, weighted and adaptive variants — is an attempt to live well inside it.

## What changed

Conformal prediction spent two decades as a mostly theoretical program and has, in the last few years, become deployment infrastructure: uncertainty sets on clinical triage models, abstention rules for retrieval and generation, calibrated risk bands in forecasting pipelines. The failure mode this creates is specific. A team wraps a model in split conformal, checks empirical coverage on held-out data, sees $0.902$, and ships. The number is correct and the system is still broken for the subpopulation that actually needed the uncertainty estimate — because that subpopulation is where the model is uncertain, which is exactly where a marginal guarantee spends its error budget.

The literature has known this since at least Vovk's 2012 taxonomy of conditional validity. What is new is the number of systems in which it matters.

## The rank argument, and what it averages over

Fix a score function $s(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}$, larger meaning worse agreement between $y$ and the model's belief about $x$. Fit the model on a training split, then compute scores $s_i = s(X_i, Y_i)$ on a disjoint calibration set of size $n$. Let

$$\hat{q} = \text{the } \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil \text{-th smallest of } s_1, \dots, s_n,$$

and predict $\hat{C}(x) = { y : s(x, y) \le \hat{q} }$.

The proof is one line of symmetry. If $(X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_{n+1}, Y_{n+1})$ are exchangeable and the model was fit without touching any of them, the scores $s_1, \dots, s_{n+1}$ are exchangeable too. With ties broken almost surely, the rank of $s_{n+1}$ among all $n+1$ scores is uniform on ${1, \dots, n+1}$. Coverage fails exactly when that rank exceeds $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$, so

$$1 - \alpha \le \mathbb{P}\big(Y_{n+1} \in \hat{C}(X_{n+1})\big) \le 1 - \alpha + \frac{1}{n+1}.$$

Lei, G'Sell, Rinaldo, Tibshirani and Wasserman give the full treatment of this and its full-conformal and jackknife relatives.

Notice what the probability integrates over: the calibration draw, the test label, *and the test covariate*. Two distinct weakenings hide there. Averaging over $X_{n+1}$ gives the marginal-versus-conditional problem. Averaging over the calibration set gives the training-conditional problem — the guarantee describes the average calibration set, not yours, and you only ever draw one.

## Why conditional coverage is not merely hard

The target you actually want is $$\mathbb{P}\big(Y \in \hat{C}(X) \mid X = x\big) \ge 1 - \alpha \quad \text{for (almost) every } x.$$

Barber, Candès, Ramdas and Tibshirani settle this. Any procedure with distribution-free conditional validity must, for every distribution $P$, produce sets whose expected Lebesgue measure is infinite at almost every non-atom of $P_X$. The result traces back to Vovk (2012) and Lei and Wasserman (2014); the 2021 paper sharpens it and then maps the space of achievable relaxations.

The intuition is worth stating plainly, because "impossibility theorem" invites people to assume a pathological construction. It is not pathological. Conditioning on $X = x$ at a continuous covariate means you have, almost surely, seen that point zero times. Producing a finite interval that is valid at $x$ *for every distribution* would require extracting local information about $P_{Y|X=x}$ from data that contains none, unless you are willing to borrow strength from neighbouring $x$ — and borrowing strength is a smoothness assumption, which is precisely what distribution-free forbids.

So the impossibility is a statement about the target under the constraint, not a defect in conformal prediction. Read correctly it is liberating: it tells you to stop looking for the method that delivers exact conditional coverage and start choosing which relaxation you want.

Two relaxations are worth your time.

**Discretize the conditioning.** Fix a partition of the covariate space into finitely many groups, calibrate a separate $\hat{q}_g$ within each, and you get exact group-conditional coverage, at the cost of $1/(n_g + 1)$ slack per group and the requirement that the partition be fixed in advance. This is Vovk's Mondrian construction. It is the correct default whenever you can name the axis you care about — class label in imbalanced classification, site in multi-site clinical data, language in multilingual NLP.

**Fix the score, not the guarantee.** The theorem constrains what you can *prove*, not how the procedure behaves. Two score functions with identical marginal guarantees can have wildly different conditional behaviour, and this is where nearly all practical progress lives.

## The arithmetic of an easy majority

Take the residual score $s(x,y) = |y - \hat{\mu}(x)|$. It yields $\hat{C}(x) = [\hat{\mu}(x) - \hat{q}, \hat{\mu}(x) + \hat{q}]$ — a band of *constant width* regardless of $x$. Under any heteroscedasticity, this is a disaster wearing a valid guarantee.

Here is the cleanest way I know to see how bad. Suppose a fraction $\pi$ of your population is easy enough that the fitted band covers it essentially always, and the remaining $1 - \pi$ is hard. Marginal coverage decomposes as $\pi \cdot 1 + (1 - \pi) \cdot c = 1 - \alpha$, so the hard subpopulation receives

$$c = \frac{(1 - \alpha) - \pi}{1 - \pi}.$$

At $\alpha = 0.1$: if half your data is easy, the hard half gets 80%. If 80% is easy, the hard 20% gets 50%. If 90% is easy, the hard tenth gets *zero* — a nominal 90% interval that never covers a tenth of your users, while the validation dashboard reads 0.90.

Concretely, let $Y = \mu(X) + \sigma(X)\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)$, $\mu$ known, and $\sigma(X) = 1$ on half the population and $4$ on the other half. Solving $\Phi(\hat{q}) + \Phi(\hat{q}/4) = 1.9$ gives $\hat{q} \approx 5.13$. Conditional coverage is $2\Phi(5.13) - 1 \approx 1.000$ on the low-noise half and $2\Phi(1.28) - 1 \approx 0.800$ on the high-noise half. Widening the noise ratio does not help; it pins the hard group at 80% and just makes the interval more absurdly wide for the easy group.

Conformalized quantile regression, from Romano, Patterson and Candès, changes the score rather than the calibration. Fit conditional quantile estimates $\hat{q}*{\alpha/2}(x)$ and $\hat{q}*{1-\alpha/2}(x)$, then use

$$s(x, y) = \max\big{\hat{q}*{\alpha/2}(x) - y,; y - \hat{q}*{1-\alpha/2}(x)\big},$$

giving $\hat{C}(x) = [\hat{q}*{\alpha/2}(x) - \hat{q},; \hat{q}*{1-\alpha/2}(x) + \hat{q}]$. The width now varies with $x$ through the quantile estimates, and the conformal step only applies a global correction for their miscalibration. The marginal guarantee is identical; the conditional behaviour is not remotely identical. The classification analogue is the adaptive prediction sets of Romano, Sesia and Candès, which accumulate sorted class probabilities rather than thresholding the top one, producing larger sets exactly where the model is diffuse.

A sketch that makes the contrast reproducible:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
grp = rng.integers(0, 2, 2 * n)              # 0 = easy, 1 = hard
sig = np.where(grp == 0, 1.0, 4.0)
y = rng.normal(0.0, sig)                     # mu(x) = 0, known
cal, test = slice(0, n), slice(n, 2 * n)
# residual score -> constant-width band
q = np.quantile(np.abs(y[cal]), np.ceil(0.9 * (n + 1)) / n, method="higher")
cov = np.abs(y[test]) <= q
# CQR with oracle quantiles -> width scales with sigma
lo, hi = norm.ppf(0.05) * sig, norm.ppf(0.95) * sig
s = np.maximum(lo[cal] - y[cal], y[cal] - hi[cal])
qc = np.quantile(s, np.ceil(0.9 * (n + 1)) / n, method="higher")
covc = (y[test] >= lo[test] - qc) & (y[test] <= hi[test] + qc)
for name, c in [("residual", cov), ("CQR", covc)]:
    g = grp[test]
    print(name, round(c.mean(), 3), round(c[g == 0].mean(), 3), round(c[g == 1].mean(), 3))
```

Both rows report marginal coverage near $0.90$. Only one reports group coverages near $0.90$.

## When exchangeability itself goes

Everything above assumes exchangeable scores. Deployment routinely breaks that, and the literature splits by how much structure you are willing to claim.

If the shift is pure covariate shift with a known or well-estimated likelihood ratio $w(x) = dP_{\text{test}}/dP_{\text{train}}(x)$, Tibshirani, Barber, Candès and Ramdas show that replacing the empirical quantile with a *weighted* quantile — calibration point $i$ receiving mass proportional to $w(X_i)$, the test point receiving mass proportional to $w(x)$ — restores exact coverage. The machinery generalizes to a weighted notion of exchangeability. The catch is that $w$ must come from somewhere, typically a density-ratio classifier on unlabeled test covariates, and there is no distribution-free way to check that you got it right.

If you cannot claim that much, the nonexchangeable conformal of Barber, Candès, Ramdas and Tibshirani (2023) gives a bound rather than a guarantee: with normalized weights $\tilde{w}_i$,

$$(1 - \alpha) - \mathbb{P}\big(Y_{n+1} \in \hat{C}*{n+1}\big) ;\le; \sum*{i=1}^{n} \tilde{w}*i , d*{\text{TV}}\big(Z, Z^i\big),$$

where $Z^i$ is the data sequence with the test point and the $i$-th calibration point swapped. The bound is zero under exchangeability, so downweighting stale points is free insurance; under drift it converts an unquantified risk into a quantity you can at least reason about, even if the total variation distances are not observable.

And if you are online with feedback, Gibbs and Candès's adaptive conformal inference abandons the fixed level entirely, updating

$$\alpha_{t+1} = \alpha_t + \gamma\big(\alpha - \text{err}_t\big),$$

with $\text{err}_t$ the indicator of miscoverage at time $t$. This delivers long-run empirical coverage converging to $1 - \alpha$ under essentially arbitrary drift, which is a real and useful guarantee — and a completely different one. It says nothing about time $t$. The interval you show a user tomorrow has no guarantee attached to it.

## What to actually do

Stop reporting marginal coverage as evidence that conformal is working. It is evidence that your code is correct. Report coverage stratified by every axis you would be embarrassed to fail on — class, site, demographic group, input length, model confidence decile — and treat the worst slice as the headline number.

Default to an adaptive score. CQR for regression, APS for classification, or at minimum a normalized residual $|y - \hat{\mu}(x)| / \hat{\sigma}(x)$ with a fitted scale model. The residual score should be a deliberate choice for genuinely homoscedastic problems, not the thing you reach for because it is one line.

Use Mondrian calibration on any axis where you can name the groups and afford the per-group sample size — and check $n_g$, because the $1/(n_g+1)$ slack that is invisible at $n = 5000$ is a live problem for a rare class with $n_g = 40$.

Choose $n$ so that $(n+1)\alpha$ is an integer, which makes the upper bound tight rather than merely close. And keep calibration data genuinely untouched: if you selected a model, tuned a threshold, or picked a score using those points, the scores are no longer exchangeable and you have no guarantee at all — only a number.

## What this does not settle

The impossibility result is about the worst case over all $P$. Under smoothness or margin conditions you can get asymptotic conditional coverage, and those conditions are often plausible. But you have then left the distribution-free setting, and the guarantee is worth exactly what the assumption is worth — which is a judgment call, not a theorem.

Training-conditional validity is the weakening people most often miss. Bian and Barber show that split conformal does satisfy a training-conditional guarantee, while full conformal and jackknife+ provably do not without further assumptions. Since real pipelines calibrate once and deploy for months, this is a live argument for split conformal over its more sample-efficient cousins — a tradeoff that gets stated backwards fairly often.

Two things I think are genuinely open, marked as my own reading rather than anyone's claim. First, group-conditional coverage over a *rich, overlapping* family of groups sits awkwardly between the achievable finite-partition case and the impossible pointwise case, and the practical guidance for choosing that family is thin. Second, for generative models the conditioning problem compounds: the label is not a point but a set of acceptable outputs, so "conditional coverage" needs a definition before it can be relaxed, and I have not seen a treatment I find convincing.

The honest summary is narrower than the marketing. Conformal prediction does not make an uncertain model informative. It makes a model's uncertainty *honest on average*, and gives you precise, well-characterized tools for choosing which average.

[proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/8fb21ee7a2207526da55a679f0332de2-Abstract.html](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/8fb21ee7a2207526da55a679f0332de2-Abstract.html) — weighted exchangeability, and the cleanest statement of what a likelihood ratio buys you.

- Gibbs, Candès, *Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift*, NeurIPS 2021. [proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/hash/0d441de75945e5acbc865406fc9a2559-Abstract.html](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/hash/0d441de75945e5acbc865406fc9a2559-Abstract.html) — online calibration under drift; note carefully what the long-run guarantee does and does not cover.
